claims.text: Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 is proposed as the carbon-free baseline alloy.
The carbon-free phosphorus-containing baseline has limited glass-forming ability under standard rapid-quenching conditions.
Carbon should be introduced during alloy synthesis as the intervention.
Carbon doping will improve the glass-forming ability of phosphorus-containing high-entropy alloys.
Carbon doping will enhance the thermal stability of the amorphous state in phosphorus-containing high-entropy alloys.
Rapid quenching, such as melt-spinning, can provide conditions under which amorphization is attainable in phosphorus-containing alloys.
Carbon must be maintained within an optimal concentration range for the beneficial effect to occur.
Excessive carbon will promote secondary-phase formation or phase separation.
Carbon substitution or interstitial incorporation will increase local structural disorder and modify bonding environments.
The carbon-induced local disorder and bonding changes will disrupt crystalline nucleation and growth.
Carbon doping will elevate the alloy's configurational entropy.
Carbon-induced bonding heterogeneity will lower the nucleation rate of crystalline phases.
Suppression of crystalline nucleation will stabilize the amorphous structure against thermal crystallization.
Relative to an otherwise equivalent carbon-free alloy, the carbon-doped alloy will have a greater amorphous phase fraction or propensity to form an amorphous structure.
Relative to the carbon-free control, the carbon-doped alloy will have a higher crystallization-onset temperature.
The benefit may disappear when cooling rates are insufficient to suppress crystallization.
Carbon doping has previously been implicated in increasing the glass-forming ability of a related Cantor-composition system.
The optimal carbon concentration and magnitude of thermal stabilization in phosphorus-containing high-entropy alloys are uncertain.

Failure of carbon-doped samples to show either a statistically significant increase in amorphous fraction or a higher crystallization-onset temperature than the carbon-free control would falsify the hypothesis.
